output.title: Early signs your AI workflow is drifting
output.body:
Eval drift is not a theory problem for a small business; it is a workflow problem. If an AI-assisted process starts giving answers that are inconsistent, off-target, or just a bit too confident, the question is not whether the model has become sentient. It is whether the workflow still deserves to stay on autopilot.

The practical check is simple: do you already have one repetitive, high-frequency task where AI filters, ranks, or responds to inputs, and would drift show up as customer complaints, missed approvals, failed orders, or manual rework? If the answer is no, there is nothing to monitor yet. If the answer is yes, pick one control and write it down.

A sensible first control is a manual monthly spot-check against a small set of past cases using the original success criteria. Keep the comparison human-readable: what came in, what the system output, and whether a person would still sign off on it. Any threshold you use should be your own operating rule, not a Bareni benchmark.

In a free 30-minute diagnostic, the useful question is: “Is eval drift a real risk in this workflow, or are we trying to solve a problem we do not have yet?” That keeps the decision bounded. If drift monitoring belongs anywhere, it belongs inside a pilot scope with human approval before any retraining or policy change. Small business automation works better when it fails politely, not mysteriously.
